subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
passage:
"Avni ma'am, look at that boy in lane four. His arms go so smooth."
"That's front crawl. What do you notice?"
"His hand goes in near his head. Then it pushes back all the way to his leg."
"Good. Try it here, standing on the poolside."
Joseph swung his arms, one after the other.
"Now in the water. I'm watching."
He pushed off and swung his arms the same way. Water splashed everywhere.
"Stop. Joseph, your elbow is straight, like a windmill. His elbow bends and stays high. Try again."
"Like this?"
"Higher. Yes. Feel the difference?"
"It's quieter. And I'm faster!"

qa.q: Which lane was the older swimmer in?
qa.a: He was in lane four.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when he said, "It's quieter. And I'm faster!"?
qa.a: He felt excited and pleased, noticing the difference the bent elbow made.

qa.q: What else could Joseph do to keep improving his stroke?
qa.a: He could practise one arm at a time holding a float, because focusing on one arm makes the elbow easier to control.

qa.q: How does Joseph's copying look to Avni ma'am?
qa.a: Avni ma'am is happy he is watching carefully, and sees that copying works best when she checks and corrects it.

grounding: It shows a boy watching an older swimmer's arm movement, copying it on the poolside and in the water, and the coach fixing his elbow.

subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
passage: At the club pool I watched the older swimmers for a whole week before I tried anything. One boy's arms fascinated me. They came out of the water bent at the elbow, reached forward, went in without a splash. On Saturday I stood on the poolside and copied him slowly in the air. Right arm, left arm, head to the side to breathe. Then I got in and tried it with Anand sir watching. "Your elbow is dropping, Jomon," he said. "Keep it high, like you're reaching over a fence." I tried again. It felt awkward, then it felt right. I'm still slow, but now my arms look a little like his, and I don't splash the whole lane.

qa.q: What did Anand sir say was dropping?
qa.a: He said Jomon's elbow was dropping.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when the new movement first felt awkward?
qa.a: Jomon felt unsure and a bit clumsy, and then pleased when it started to feel right.

qa.q: What else could Jomon try to check his arms without a coach?
qa.a: Jomon could ask a friend to take a short video at the poolside, so the elbow can be checked later.

qa.q: How might the older swimmer see Jomon copying him?
qa.a: The older swimmer might be surprised or flattered that someone was watching his stroke so closely.

grounding: It shows a child watching an older swimmer's arm strokes, copying them on the poolside and in the water while the coach corrects the elbow.

subtype: Approach: practising only with a float and never without [Pitfall]
passage: For six weeks at swimming class I held the blue kickboard every single time. With it, I felt safe. Without it, I felt like the water would swallow me. Coach said, "Try letting go in the shallow end. I'm right here." I always said, "Next week." My friend Zainab let go in the third week and was swimming widths by the fifth. On Saturday the coach announced a small test: one width, no board. Everyone lined up. I stood there, hugging the board to my chest. "Rekha, just try," Zainab whispered. I couldn't. I watched them all go across. I was the only girl still holding a board. I went home and didn't talk at dinner.

qa.q: How many weeks had Rekha held the kickboard?
qa.a: Rekha had held it for six weeks.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel watching the others swim across?
qa.a: Rekha felt stuck and ashamed, the only one still holding a board, and was quiet all through dinner.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Rekha let go, and why?
qa.a: Let go for just two seconds in the shallow end with the coach's hand close, because a tiny safe try is less scary than a whole width.

qa.q: How does Rekha's week look to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab wants Rekha to succeed and whispers encouragement, and probably feels sad for a friend who is stuck.

grounding: It shows a girl who always holds a kickboard because it feels safe, and after weeks still cannot swim alone because she never let go.

subtype: Approach: practising only with a float and never without [Pitfall]
passage:
Coach's note, beginners' group, week eight
Neelam comes to every lesson and kicks hard, but she has not let go of her float once in eight weeks. When I suggest it, even in the shallow end where she can stand, she says, "Not today." This week the group swam their first full width without floats. Neelam watched from the side, holding hers, and her eyes filled up. She is not lazy; she is afraid, and the float has become a wall. Next week I will stand beside her in waist-deep water and ask her to let go for a count of three while holding my arm. I have also asked Tejas, her swim buddy, to practise the count with her.
- Coach

qa.q: How many weeks has Neelam held the float?
qa.a: She has held it for eight weeks.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling as she watched from the side?
qa.a: She was upset and afraid, with her eyes filling up as the others swam without floats.

qa.q: What does the coach's plan get right, and what else could help?
qa.a: It makes the step tiny and safe, a count of three while holding an arm; adding a little each week could help Neelam build trust.

qa.q: How might Tejas see being asked to help Neelam?
qa.a: Tejas may feel trusted and want to help a buddy, while also learning patience.

grounding: It shows a girl who always practises with a float, and after weeks still cannot swim alone because she never tried letting go.

subtype: Approach: swimming only when a trained adult is watching [Thinking]
passage: Francis's friends in their Mumbai building were planning a Sunday trip to the beach. "We'll swim at the rocks," said Raghav. "Nobody's there. It's the best part." Francis had been having swimming lessons for a year. He was a good swimmer. But he thought about the coach saying the sea is not a pool: waves, currents, no edges. "Is there a lifeguard at the rocks?" "No, that's why it's quiet." Francis shook his head. "Then I'll swim at the main beach, where the lifeguard is. You can come too." Raghav rolled his eyes. "You swim better than all of us." "That's why I know the sea's different," said Francis. "It's part of my plan, not a rule someone gave me."

qa.q: Where did Raghav want to swim?
qa.a: Raghav wanted to swim at the rocks.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Raghav rolled his eyes?
qa.a: He felt calm and sure, not ashamed, because he saw the choice as his own plan.

qa.q: What else could Francis do to help the group stay safe?
qa.a: He could suggest they tell a parent where they are going and all swim near the lifeguard, so the plan includes everyone.

qa.q: How does Francis's choice look to Raghav?
qa.a: Raghav thinks it is too careful for such a good swimmer, and may be a little annoyed at first.

grounding: It shows a child who understands that open water is dangerous and decides to swim only where a trained adult lifeguard is watching, as part of his plan.

subtype: Approach: swimming only when a trained adult is watching [Thinking]
passage:
"Vikas, the boys are going to the river after school. Are you going?"
"No, Sunaina didi."
"But you love swimming."
"In the pool. With the coach there."
"The river's calm today. I saw it."
"Calm on top. Coach says rivers pull from underneath, and there's nobody to pull you out."
"So you'll never swim in a river?"
"Not without a grown-up who's trained. That's my plan. It's not a punishment. It's how I keep swimming."
"And if they call you scared?"
"Then they call me scared. I'll ask Papa if we can go to the river on Sunday, where the lifeguard stands."

qa.q: What does Vikas say the coach told him about rivers?
qa.a: That rivers pull from underneath and there's nobody to pull you out.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel about being called scared?
qa.a: He seems calm and settled about it, because he sees staying safe as his own plan.

qa.q: What else could Vikas do to enjoy the water with his friends?
qa.a: He could invite the boys to the pool session or to the guarded river spot on Sunday, so they swim together safely.

qa.q: How does Vikas's decision look to Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina is surprised at first, but his clear reasons probably reassure her.

grounding: It shows a child choosing never to go into water without a trained adult lifeguard and treating that as part of his plan, not a limit.

subtype: Approach: setting small distances as goals [Revision]
passage: Vandana, you think you're the slowest in your swimming class? Let your Parveen Nani tell you something. When I learned, at a pool in Lucknow, all the girls were faster than me. I felt like a buffalo among fish. Then one day I stopped comparing. I said, "This week, I will swim one width without stopping." That was all. It took four tries. The next week: two widths. Then three. I kept a little chart on the back of my notebook, and every Saturday I wrote the number. By the end of summer I had forty ticks on that chart. I was still not the fastest. But I could see, every week, that I was faster than me.

qa.q: What did Parveen write on the chart every Saturday?
qa.a: Parveen wrote the number of widths.

qa.q: How did young Parveen feel among the faster girls?
qa.a: Young Parveen felt slow and discouraged, like a buffalo among fish.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: The turning point was dropping the comparison and aiming for one width, because a small goal could be reached and counted.

qa.q: How might the other girls in the class have seen young Parveen?
qa.a: They may have noticed Parveen getting steadily stronger and gained some respect for that quiet progress.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling slow as a girl learning to swim, setting goals of one width and then two, and counting progress each week.

subtype: Approach: setting small distances as goals [Revision]
passage: Nandini's swimming slot at the municipal pool was only thirty minutes, and the lanes were so crowded that she spent half of it waiting. She felt she was getting nowhere. On Monday she told her friend Vidya, "I'm going to stop trying to swim fast and just try for one full width." In the next slot she swam one width without stopping, dodging a man doing backstroke. On Thursday she tried two. She kept the count on a card in her bag: Week 1: one width. Week 2: two. Week 3: three, even though the lane was packed. Vidya started keeping a card too. "It's not about how fast," Nandini told her. "It's about the number going up."

qa.q: How long was Nandini's swimming slot?
qa.a: It was only thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel before she changed her goal?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and stuck, as if she was getting nowhere in the crowded pool.

qa.q: What else could Nandini try when the lanes are packed?
qa.a: She could use the waiting time to practise breathing at the wall, so no minute of the short slot is wasted.

qa.q: How does Nandini's plan look to Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya sees it working and starts her own card, so it seems useful and encouraging to her.

grounding: It shows a girl who feels slow setting small goals of one width, then two, and counting her widths each week.

subtype: Approach: writing a list from the teacher's notice [Action]
passage: Yusuf, you want to know why your Ujjwal Chacha still reads every notice twice? Because of the museum trip, when I was a boy. The school gave us a paper circular. Most boys stuffed it in their bags. I sat on the steps and read it slowly. Packed lunch. Water bottle. Cap. School ID card. Twenty rupees for the entry ticket. I copied the five things on the back of my hand in ink, and at home onto a slip of paper. Next morning my friend Pappu forgot his ID and had to wait with the teacher at the gate. I didn't guess anything, beta. The notice told me what to bring, and I brought it.

qa.q: What was the twenty rupees for?
qa.a: It was for the entry ticket.

qa.q: How did young Ujjwal feel the next morning compared with Pappu?
qa.a: Young Ujjwal probably felt relieved and a bit proud, since Pappu had to wait at the gate while Ujjwal had everything.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference, and what else could have helped?
qa.a: Reading the circular slowly and copying the list was the key choice; Ujjwal could also have shown the list to a parent to double-check.

qa.q: How might Pappu have felt waiting with the teacher at the gate?
qa.a: Pappu probably felt embarrassed and left out while the others went in.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy, making a packing list from the school's trip notice so he did not have to guess.

subtype: Approach: writing a list from the teacher's notice [Action]
passage: The circular for the planetarium trip came home in Deepak's bag on a rainy Thursday, and by the time he found it, the ink had run. His mother, Rehana, was on a late shift, and the trip was the next morning. Deepak spread the soggy paper on the table and read what he could. "Packed lunch. Water. Cap... is that cap? ID card. Fifty rupees." He wrote each item on a clean sheet, then held the circular under the lamp to check the smudged word. It was cap. He packed each thing and ticked it off. When his mother came home at ten, the bag was by the door with the list on top. She read it, and then read the circular. "You didn't guess anything," she said.

qa.q: Why was the ink on the circular smudged?
qa.a: It was a rainy day and the ink had run.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when his mother read the list?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and relieved that he had managed it himself.

qa.q: What else could Deepak do if a word on the circular was unreadable?
qa.a: He could call a classmate or check the class message group with his mother's help, rather than guess.

qa.q: How does the packed bag look to Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana, tired after a late shift, is pleased and impressed that Deepak used the notice carefully.

grounding: It shows a boy using the teacher's circular to write a packing list so he does not have to guess.

subtype: Approach: imagining the day from morning to evening [Thinking]
passage: The night before the school trip to the old fort near Chanderi, Dilnaz lay on her mat and walked through the day in her head. "First, the bus. It'll be hot, the windows don't open. Then the climb up to the fort, in the sun." Her hand went to her forehead. "Hat. My brother's straw hat." She kept going. "Lunch on the grass. Sticky fingers." She sat up. "Tissues." "Where do the wrappers go? There's no bin at the fort." She fetched a plastic bag and folded it into her bag. Her brother Hrithik mumbled from the other mat. "Why are you talking to yourself?" "I'm on the bus," Dilnaz said, "and now I'm eating lunch."

qa.q: Whose hat did Dilnaz decide to take?
qa.a: She decided to take her brother's straw hat.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel as she worked through the day in her head?
qa.a: She felt focused and a little excited, sitting up each time she thought of something she'd need.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz do with her imagined day, and why?
qa.a: She could write each item on a list as she thinks of it, so she can check the bag in the morning.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz's planning look to Hrithik?
qa.a: Hrithik is sleepy and confused, thinking she is just talking to herself.

grounding: It shows a girl imagining the trip from bus to lunch to the ride back and adding a hat, tissues and a plastic bag for wrappers.

subtype: Approach: imagining the day from morning to evening [Thinking]
passage: The night before her class trip to the botanical gardens outside Durban, Zanele sat on her bed with her backpack open. She closed her eyes. "Morning: bus, forty minutes. I'll be thirsty. Water." She pictured walking along the paths in the sun. "Hat." She pictured lunch on the grass, sticky orange hands. "Wipes." She pictured the teacher saying no litter. "A bag for rubbish." Then the ride back, tired. "Something to read." Her friend Wanjiru called to ask what she was packing. Zanele read the list aloud. "You thought of rubbish bags?" Wanjiru said. "I'm getting one now."

qa.q: How did Zanele feel as she pictured each part of the day?
qa.a: She felt calm and thoughtful, picturing each part to be ready.

qa.q: What else could Zanele add to her plan, and why?

qa.q: How does Zanele's list look to Wanjiru?
qa.a: Wanjiru is impressed by the rubbish bag idea and decides to pack one herself.

grounding: It shows a girl mentally walking through a school trip from morning to evening and adding a hat, wipes and a rubbish bag.

subtype: Approach: packing at the last minute in a hurry [Pitfall]
passage: Jatin's alarm rang at six. He turned it off. At six-thirty his mother, Nikita, shook him. "The bus is at seven!" He leapt up and stuffed things in his bag: tiffin, a jumper, a comic. He couldn't find his socks, then his shoes. At six-fifty-five he ran down the stairs of their building in Thane. The bus was at the gate. He was halfway up the steps when the teacher asked, "Permission slip?" Jatin's stomach dropped. It was on the fridge. And his water bottle was on the kitchen counter. His mother came flying down the stairs in her nightdress and slippers, the slip in one hand, the bottle in the other.

qa.q: What time was the bus due?
qa.a: The bus was due at seven.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when the teacher asked for the permission slip?
qa.a: He felt a sinking panic, his stomach dropping, as he remembered it was on the fridge.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Jatin better, and why?
qa.a: Packing the night before with a list, because checking calmly catches things like the slip and the bottle.

qa.q: How does the morning look to Nikita?
qa.a: Nikita has to run downstairs in her nightdress, so she is probably flustered and a little annoyed.

grounding: It shows a child starting to pack half an hour before the bus, forgetting the permission slip and water bottle, and his mother running to the gate.

subtype: Approach: packing at the last minute in a hurry [Pitfall]
passage:
"Shankar! It's six-thirty! Your bus is at seven!"
"I know, Amma, I'm packing!"
"You said you'd pack last night."
"I was tired! Harish, have you seen my cap?"
"It's on the fan. Why is it on the fan?"
"Never mind! Tiffin, tiffin, where's the tiffin?"
"In your hand."
"Oh."
"Shankar, the bus is honking!"
"Bye!"
Shankar grabbed his bag and the door slammed. Harish looked at the table. The signed permission slip. The water bottle.
"Amma..."
Amma grabbed both and ran down the stairs in her slippers, waving at the bus as it started to move.

qa.a: It was on the fan.

qa.q: How was Shankar feeling while he packed?

qa.q: How does the rush look to Harish?
qa.a: Harish watches the chaos calmly and is the one who notices the slip and bottle left on the table.

grounding: It shows a child packing in a hurry half an hour before the bus, forgetting his permission slip and water bottle, and his mother running out with them.

subtype: Approach: keeping the bag light and taking only what is needed [Thinking]
passage: My neighbour Harsha was going on the class trip to the lake, and on the evening before, I was helping his mother fold clothes on their balcony when he came out with two bags. The big one had his whole toy car collection, three books and a board game. The small one had a water bottle and a cap. He stood there looking at both. "Last year I took the big bag to the zoo," he said, mostly to himself, "and my shoulders hurt all day and I couldn't run." He took the cars out. Then the books. He put his lunch and a jacket into the small bag. I don't know if he was sad about the cars. He looked lighter, somehow.

qa.q: What was in Harsha's big bag?
qa.a: His whole toy car collection, three books and a board game.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling as he took the cars out?
qa.a: He may have felt a little sad to leave them but also relieved about carrying less, though the neighbour can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Harsha do if he wants something to play with on the trip?
qa.a: He could take one small toy that fits in a pocket, so he has fun without a heavy load.

qa.q: How does Harsha's choice look to his mother?
qa.a: His mother would likely be pleased that he remembered last year and planned a lighter bag.

grounding: It shows a boy recalling that a heavy bag tired him last time and choosing to leave toys and extra books for a small bag he can carry.

subtype: Approach: keeping the bag light and taking only what is needed [Thinking]
passage:
Wednesday: On the zoo trip, Rafiq's backpack was so heavy that by lunchtime he was dragging it along the path. His friend Sarika raced ahead to see the tigers. Rafiq sat on a bench, shoulders aching.
The next Monday: The school sent a notice for a nature walk on Friday. Rafiq looked at his big backpack. "Last time I carried everything and saw nothing," he thought. He found his small cloth bag.
Thursday: He packed water, a cap, lunch and a notebook. He left out the comics, the torch, the extra jumper. "Enough," he said.
Friday: On the nature walk he kept up with Sarika the whole way and was the first to spot a kingfisher.

qa.q: What bird did Rafiq spot first on Friday?
qa.a: He spotted a kingfisher.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel sitting on the bench at the zoo?

qa.q: How does the lighter bag look to Sarika?

subtype: Approach: packing the day before and checking twice [Action]

subtype: Approach: packing the day before and checking twice [Action]
passage: Last month our class went on a day trip to the tea gardens, and I finally tried packing the night before, the way my aunt does. After dinner I laid everything on my bed: water bottle, tiffin box, raincoat, sun cap, notebook, and my bus pass. I put each thing in and ticked it. Then I went to sleep, which I never do before trips. In the morning, while my friend Dolma was already waiting at the gate, I checked the list one more time. The sun cap was not in the bag. I'd taken it out to try on and left it on the chair. I put it back. I went down feeling calm, not rushing. Dolma had forgotten her cap. I, Ishita, lent her my spare, and she said, "Thank you, didi."

qa.q: Where did Ishita find the sun cap?
qa.a: It was on the chair, taken out to try on.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel going down to the gate?
qa.a: Ishita felt calm, not rushed, having checked everything twice.

qa.q: What would help Ishita if there was no time for a morning check?
qa.a: Ishita could put the bag right by the door after the night check, so nothing gets taken out and forgotten.

qa.q: How does the morning look to Dolma?
qa.a: Dolma, who forgot her cap, is grateful that Ishita has a spare to lend.

subtype: Approach: taking everything he might possibly need [Pitfall]
passage: Yash, you want to take three bags on a one-day trip? Let your Yusuf Nana tell you a story. When I was a boy, our school went to the zoo, and I was so worried about everything that might go wrong. What if I got hungry? Three snacks. What if it got cold? Two jackets. What if it got dark? The big torch from the store room. My bag was so heavy I walked sideways. At the school gate, my teacher lifted it and her eyebrows went up. "Yusuf, are you moving house?" She made me leave half of it in the classroom. I was angry that day. But without all that weight, I climbed up to the bird house with everyone else.

qa.q: What did young Yusuf take in case it got dark?
qa.a: The big torch from the store room.

qa.q: How did young Yusuf feel when the teacher made him leave half?
qa.a: Young Yusuf felt angry, though later glad to climb with everyone else.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the day better, and what could Yusuf have done instead?
qa.a: Leaving half at school was the turning point; Yusuf could have asked what was really needed and packed only that.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen the heavy bag?
qa.a: The teacher was surprised and a little amused, but also worried he wouldn't manage it all day.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy worried about what might go wrong, packing too much and having to leave half at school.

subtype: Approach: taking everything he might possibly need [Pitfall]
passage: Hrithik had packed for the school trip to the hill fort as if he were leaving for a month: three snack boxes, two jackets, a big torch, a first-aid tin, a book, and a board game. It was already hot and the bus was late. When his teacher, Salma ma'am, lifted his bag onto the bus steps, she nearly dropped it. "Hrithik, what if you can't carry this up the hill?" He had worried about everything except that. She asked him to keep one snack, one jacket and water, and leave the rest in the staffroom. He felt his face go red. But at the top of the hill, sweaty and puffing, he was glad his bag was light, and nobody asked about his torch.

qa.q: How many snack boxes did Hrithik pack?
qa.a: He packed three snack boxes.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel when Salma ma'am asked him to leave things behind?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face going red, since he had worried about everything except the weight.

qa.q: What else could Hrithik try next time he feels worried about what might go wrong?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher or a parent which worries are real, and pack one item for each instead of several.

qa.q: How does the heavy bag look to Salma ma'am?
qa.a: Salma ma'am sees a worried boy about to struggle up a hill, so she kindly helps him cut down.

grounding: It shows a boy so worried about what might go wrong that he packs far too much, and the teacher asks him to leave half at school.
